blocks.text: “For the others [this mental enstasis without an object] is preceded by serene confidence, energy, watchful attention, cessation, and prajñā ‘perfect sapience’.” 615

Upāya-pratyayo yoginām bhavati 616 / Śraddhā cetasaḥ samprasādaḥ / Sā hi jananī_iva kalyāṇī yoginaṃ pāti / Tasya hi śraddadhānasya 617 viveka-arthino vīryam upajāyate / Samupajātā 618 -vīryasya smṛtir upatiṣṭhate / Smṛty-upasthāne ca 619 cittam anākulaṃ samādhiyate / Samāhita-cittasya prajñā-viveka upāvartate / Yena yathārthaṃ vastu jānāti / Tad-abhyāsāt tad-viṣayāc ca vairāgyād asaṃprajñātaḥ samādhir bhavati 620 /20/

[The other enstasis, the one without a mental object], caused by techniques, is attained by yogins. Śraddhā 621 is serenity of mind. It protects the yogin like a good mother. Energy arises in him [whose mind] is serene (and) whose goal is discrimination [between the puruṣa-subject and the psychic-object] 622 . In one who has developed energy, watchful attention arises, and when watchful attention is applied, the unperturbed psyche is led to cessation. In one whose mind is completely at rest, the climax of knowledge appears, a climax thanks to which [the yogin] knows the object as it is 623 . Due to the constant practice of these [means] and to the detachment which is their objective, non-cognitive mental enstasis occurs. /20/

615 This list coincides with that of the five indriya or bala of Buddhism. Cf. L. DE LA VALLÉE POUSSIN 1937: 228. In this Buddhist context, smṛti is not memory, but presence of mind, watchful attention.
620 MAAS 2006a: 32 lit. iti instead of bhavati.

621 In Vedic vocabulary, śraddhā is confidence in the efficacy of the rite and in the capability of the officiating priests, which is supposed to dwell within the yajamāna ‘sacrificer’, the couple who, paying for the rite, are its beneficiaries. Without this confidence, this faith, the yajña is ineffective. The hymn ṚS X.151 is dedicated to it. Here, if one believes the Bhāṣya, the meaning of śraddhā would be ‘serenity of mind’, which is thus a technical meaning specific to the work.

622 This viveka is not an action, but a state of affairs. The mind cannot discriminate between itself and a reality, the puruṣa, i.e., consciousness, which is different from itself. Everything it will ever know will never be anything other than itself. On the other hand, according to the logic of the text, there is a state where, the mind being completely at rest and thus knowing nothing, the puruṣa and the mind are discriminated. It is this state named here viveka that the yogin seeks.

623 Commentators disagree on how to understand the nature of this object; for some, it is any object whatsoever; for others, it is an important ‘object’ (center of energy, etc.) or even a venerable one (divine statue, etc.).
